The word 'yaʾas' means for most exegetes 'to know', some tracing it to the tribes of Hawazin or Nakha', while al-Farra' rejects this and some read 'yatabayyan' instead. As for the 'calamity' (qari'a), most take it to mean the raiding expeditions sent by the Prophet ﷺ, and 'the promise of God' is usually the conquest of Mecca, though al-Hasan says it is the Day of Judgment. The scholars conclude that the passage consoles the Prophet ﷺ and that God never breaks His promise.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ by reminding him that earlier messengers were also mocked, and that their peoples were not spared. The commentators explain that "amlaytu" means granting respite and prolonging the time, and that "imla'" is leaving the disbelievers for a while in ease and security, like an animal left to graze. "Thumma akhadhtuhum" means that God seized them, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand as punishment in this world by killing and in the next by the Fire. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir see the verse as a warning to the mockers and an answer to their demands for signs made in derision. The question "how was My punishment?" is, for most, an expression of wonder at what befell them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress that the respite is a gradual trap, not impunity. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that God gives the wrongdoer rope before seizing him. The linguistic sense of "mala", duration, is illustrated by al-Tabari through the word "al-malawan", night and day. Several commentators, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, link the verse to the preceding ones, where the Quraysh request miracles, and they report the occasions of revelation tied to that demand. On the details of context the opinions differ, but the commentators agree that God grants the disbelievers a respite and then seizes them, and that their punishment is severe.

This verse states that the One who watches over every soul and knows what it has earned, good or bad, and repays it, is not like the powerless idols that the idolaters made into partners of God. The answer is left out because the context implies it: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as: like their idols, which neither hear, see nor benefit anyone, while Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as: is the One who has power and unity to be deemed worthy of worship, or inanimate objects? The word qa'im is explained by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi as the one who provides sustenance and lifespans and who counts deeds for reward; al-Sam'ani and al-Mawardi add the sense of knower, and al-Mawardi reports from al-Dahhak that it could mean the angels assigned to humans, a view al-Alusi finds unlikely. For al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, the following phrases are a rebuke: 'Name them' is addressed to those who only name things that have some reality. On 'a mere apparent saying', Mujahid takes it as conjecture, Qatada and al-Dahhak as falsehood, al-Suddi as the Qur'an, and al-Tabari as something heard but without real basis. Readers differ on 'wa-suddu': some read it so that God is the one who turns them away, others that they turned themselves or others away, and al-Tabari judges the two readings close in meaning. The punishment in this world is explained as killing, capture or affliction, and the punishment of the Hereafter is said to be harder; whoever God leads astray has no guide.

This verse states that those who turn others away from God's path will face punishment in this world, that the punishment of the Hereafter is harder, and that they have no protector against God's punishment. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan explain that the worldly punishment means killing, captivity and the afflictions that befall them, and al-Tabari presents it as a divine punishment for their disbelief. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in which the Prophet said that the punishment of this world is lighter than that of the Hereafter. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud include ordinary calamities, whereas al-Razi restricts the phrase to killing, plunder, captivity and cursing. For al-Razi, the greater severity of the future punishment lies in its intensity, the variety of its forms, the absence of any relief and its endlessness. All agree that the word 'wāqin' means a protector or a shield. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan analyse the grammar of the two uses of 'min', and al-Alusi offers other readings. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse continues the earlier warning. Al-Razi cites this passage as evidence for the Sunni view that God is the one who misguides and turns people away, while the Mu'tazilites attribute this to the devil or to people themselves. The passage closes by describing the garden promised to the God-fearing, set against the punishment of the disbelievers.

This verse describes the Garden promised to the God-fearing, which the commentators present as a description of extraordinary beauty, rare in its qualities. Rivers flow beneath it, its fruit is everlasting and its shade endures. This is the final outcome of those who guarded themselves against God by avoiding what He forbade and doing what He commanded, while the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.

The commentators agree on the contrast between the destiny of the righteous and that of the disbelievers, and on the meaning of the permanence of the fruit and shade: the bliss of Paradise neither ends nor fails. Ibn Kathir notes that this answers the Jahmiyya, who claimed that the delights of Paradise would perish. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the shade is lasting because the sun does not cancel it as it does the shade of this world, and al-Shawkani reports a similar reading from Ibn Abbas.

Grammarians differ on the role of the word "mathal". Sibawayh takes it as a subject whose predicate is omitted, while al-Khalil and others make "rivers flow beneath it" the predicate. Al-Farra' regards "mathal" as an added emphatic word, and al-Zajjaj proposes the sense of a garden through which rivers flow. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejects several of these readings, and al-Razi discusses whether Paradise has already been created without settling the question.

The verse is a general description that other passages of the Qur'an and traditions elaborate. Al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri read it as an encouragement to the righteous and a warning to the disbelievers, while Ibn 'Ashur links it to the preceding mention of punishment, of which it is the counterpart.

The verse says that those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, rejoice in what has been sent down to the Prophet ﷺ because it agrees with their own scriptures, while some of the factions, meaning the disbelievers who banded together against the Prophet ﷺ, reject part of it. The commentators differ on who is meant. Qatada, Ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take those who rejoice to be the Prophet's companions or believers among the People of the Book, while Mujahid names them the believing People of the Book. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan take them to be Jewish and Christian Muslims specifically. As for the factions, Mujahid identifies them as Jews, Christians and Magians, Muqatil as the Banu Umayya and Banu al-Mughira, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan include the Quraysh and the People of the Book. Al-Wahidi, al-Qurtubi and al-Mawardi report the occasion of revelation linked to the Quran's mention of the Most Merciful, which the Quraysh rejected, a view al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi adopt. All agree on the rest of the verse: the Prophet ﷺ is to reply that he has been commanded to worship God alone without associating anything with Him, that he calls to Him, and that to Him is his return. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that rejecting this is pointless, since it is common to all revelations. On the phrase 'a judgement in Arabic', al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand the Quran revealed in the Arabic tongue, while Ibn Atiyya understands the judgement it contains. These differing views are reported without the commentators being weighed against one another.

The commentators explain that this verse compares the revelation of the Quran to the books sent to earlier prophets: it is an "Arabic judgment", meaning a wisdom and law revealed in the Arabic language, which is why it is described as Arabic. The verse then warns the Prophet ﷺ, and through him his community, that following the desires of his opponents after knowledge has come would leave him without any protector or defender against God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that these "desires" are the opinions and demands of the polytheists and the People of the Book, such as their choice of prayer direction. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Baydawi see this warning as a way of strengthening believers in their faith, since the Prophet was protected from such deviation; al-Alusi, however, holds that the warning addresses others and prefers reading "judgment" as "wisdom". Opinions also differ on the "factions": Mujahid identifies them as Jews, Christians and Magians, Muqatil as the Banu Umayya and other Quraysh, and others as the factions of pre-Islamic ignorance. The following verses are linked to this one, as the commentators report that the polytheists demanded material signs; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that no messenger brings a sign except by God's permission, and that every term has its written decree. On the meaning of erasing and confirming, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to refer to abrogated rulings, al-Hasan to the lifespans of people, while another report from Ibn 'Abbas applies it to destiny, sustenance, happiness and misery. Others restrict the erasure to matters with no reward or punishment, and some exclude happiness, misery and lifespans from its scope.

The commentators explain that this verse answers two objections raised against the Prophet ﷺ. The first concerns his marriages and children: God reminds that the messengers before him were also human beings with wives and descendants, not angels. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the objection came from the Jews or from the polytheists, who said he was only concerned with women. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim draw from it a case for marriage over celibacy, as al-Shawkani also does, citing Qatada. The second objection concerns the miracles demanded: no messenger can bring a sign except by God's permission, and for every term there is a written decree. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir take this as meaning that every matter with a fixed term has its written decree, while Ibn Kathir cites al-Dahhak, who said it means every revealed Book has its own term. On the phrase that God erases what He wills and confirms, opinions differ widely. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Tabari take it as provision, lifespans and sins; Ibn Abbas in another report and Mujahid exclude happiness, misery and death; Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Baghawi take it as the abrogation of rulings; al-Hasan takes it as the terms of life. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also record views about the recording angels and the Night of Power. As for the Mother of the Book, most identify it with the Preserved Tablet or with God's knowledge, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as the register of matters already decided, and al-Hasan as the lawful and the unlawful. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan reject the Shiite doctrine of divine change of mind (al-bada') drawn from this verse.

The commentators explain the verse 'God effaces what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book' as meaning that God removes what He wills and keeps what He wills, while the origin of the Book, which nothing in it changes, is with Him. They differ on what effacing and confirming refer to. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the abrogation of legal rulings: one command is lifted and another kept. Al-Hasan al-Basri applies it to human lifespans: whoever's term has come is removed, whoever's term has not come remains. Mujahid, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Umar extend it to provision, lifespan, happiness and misery, though Mujahid excludes happiness, misery, life and death, which do not change. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima speak of two books, one where things are erased and confirmed, and the Mother of the Book which never changes. According to al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Kalbi, the erasure concerns the recording angels' register, removing deeds with neither reward nor punishment. For the Mother of the Book, most identify it with the Preserved Tablet, the source of all writings; Ibn 'Abbas says it is the Reminder, Ka'b al-Ahbar says God's knowledge. Al-Tabari favours the view of Hasan and Mujahid, tied to the context of warning those who demanded signs. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the best reading to be the register of new matters whose outcome was decreed, and al-Razi notes that the Mother of the Book may also mean divine knowledge.

In this verse God speaks to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: whether He shows him some of the punishment He threatens the disbelievers with during his lifetime, or takes him before that, his duty is only to convey the message, while the reckoning belongs to God. The commentators read it as a consolation for the Prophet, who is not responsible for his people's faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the punishment meant is what strikes the polytheists in this world, and that the conditional clauses do not necessarily imply that the first will occur. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that Ibn Abbas and Qatada held that the phrase 'your only duty is to convey' was abrogated by the verse of the sword and the obligation of fighting, a view others do not share. On the phrase 'do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?', opinions vary. Al-Tabari, whom Ibn Kathir follows, prefers the interpretation of the Muslims' victory over the polytheists and the conquest of their lands, a view attributed to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada. Mujahid and Ikrima understood it as the ruin of the land and the death of its people, while Ata and others took it as the loss of scholars and the righteous. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the loss of blessing and fruits, and the injustice of rulers. 'None can repel His judgment' means no one rejects or overturns His decree, and He is swift in reckoning.

The verse asks the disbelievers whether they have not seen that We come to the land and reduce it from its outskirts. The commentators differ on what this reduction means. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and a group of exegetes understand it as the conquest of the unbelievers' lands by the Muslims, one land after another, a sign of the Prophet's victory; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour this reading, which al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi also support. Others, such as Mujahid, Ikrima and al-Sha'bi, take it to mean the ruin of inhabited areas, the destruction of people and the loss of fruits. Several report, through Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ata', that it means the death of scholars and the best people; al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate this view, which Ibn Abd al-Barr praises, though some find it remote from the context. On the phrase 'none can repel His judgment', all agree that no one can annul what He decides; the word mu'aqqib means one who reverses a thing and nullifies it, as Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba explain, and al-Tabari cites a line of Labid. Finally, 'swift in reckoning' means for Ibn Abbas swift in retribution, while others understand a quick and exact recompense, requiring no lengthy consideration.

This verse says that earlier peoples schemed against their prophets, and the commentators explain that makr means bringing harm to someone without his noticing. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan agree that the scheming ultimately belongs to God, who alone decides its effect, so no plot harms anyone except by His permission. They also agree that God knows what every soul earns and will repay it, and that the disbelievers will learn on the Day of Judgment to whom the good final abode belongs, namely the believers in Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari reads the clause about God's knowledge of what every soul earns as an explanation of the claim that all scheming is God's: He reaches the schemers from where they do not expect it.

Readers differ on whether the word is singular 'al-kafir', which the Kufan reading takes as a collective, or plural 'al-kuffar'. Al-Tabari prefers the plural because the surrounding speech concerns a group, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari treat the singular as a generic noun. Some report that Abu Jahl is meant, a view attributed to Ibn 'Abbas.

The next verse, about the one who has knowledge of the Book, is interpreted in several ways. Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean believing People of the Book such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Salman and Tamim al-Dari, but al-Sha'bi and Ikrima reject this because the surah is Meccan. Al-Hasan and Mujahid say it means God, Sa'id ibn Jubayr says Gabriel, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and others say Ali ibn Abi Talib. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the reading that means God weak, since it would attach a description to a proper name.

The verse relates the disbelievers' claim to the Prophet ﷺ: 'You are not a messenger.' God instructs him to answer that God suffices as a witness between him and them, since He has displayed, in support of his mission, proofs that need no other witness. The commentators agree that this witness is God's testimony to the truth of his prophethood. The identity of 'the one who has knowledge of the Book' divides them. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the people of the Scripture, Jews and Christians, who believed, foremost among them 'Abdullah ibn Salam, to whom Qatada adds Salman al-Farisi and Tamim al-Dari. Mujahid and al-Hasan take it to mean God Himself, and some read the verse with a kasra on the mim to support this view. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as the knowledge of the Qur'an and its inimitability, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies it with Gabriel. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi reject the attribution to Ibn Salam, since the sura is Meccan while his conversion took place in Medina. Ibn Kathir considers that the phrase is a collective term for the scholars of the Scripture who recognise the Prophet's description in their books. Al-Tabari adopted the majority reading and judged the alternative reading and the reports supporting it to be weak.
